Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In a previous lesson, we learned how Newton’s method works for functions of a single variable. Given a function [MATH: f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}], the method generates a sequence of approximations using the rule
[MATH: x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.]

Content:
This formula uses the derivative [MATH: f'(x_n)] to construct a local linear approximation of [MATH: f] near [MATH: x_n], which we then use to refine our guess.

Content:
In this lesson, we turn to the multivariable case, where we want to solve systems of nonlinear equations. Specifically, we are interested in finding a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n] that solves
[MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0},]
for a vector-valued function [MATH: \boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n].

Content:
The multivariable version of Newton’s method updates our guess using the formula
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),]
where [MATH: J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)] is the Jacobian matrix of [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}], evaluated at [MATH: \mathbf{x}_n].

Content:
This is a natural extension of the single-variable rule, replacing the derivative with the Jacobian and the scalar update with a vector.

Content:
To see how this method works in practice, let’s walk through a concrete example.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
Suppose we are looking for a zero of the function
[MATH: [x^{4} − y^{2} + 5; x^{2} − y^{3} + 1]]

Content:
We will perform one iteration of the Newton–Raphson method, starting from the initial guess
[MATH: [1; 1]]

Content:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function [MATH: \boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n] is

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),]

Content:
where [MATH: J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)] is the Jacobian of [MATH: \boldsymbol f] evaluated at [MATH: \mathbf{x}_n.]

Content:
In our case, the Jacobian is

Content:
[MATH: J_{f}(x)|= [(∂)/(∂x)(x^{4} − y^{2} + 5)|(∂)/(∂y)(x^{4} − y^{2} + 5); (∂)/(∂x)(x^{2} − y^{3} + 1)|(∂)/(∂y)(x^{2} − y^{3} + 1)]; = [4x^{3}|− 2y; 2x|− 3y^{2}].]

Content:
Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

Content:
[MATH: [4x^{3}|− 2y; 2x|− 3y^{2}]]

Content:
Starting with [MATH: [1; 1]] we have

Content:
[MATH: x_{1}|= x_{0} − [4x^{3}|− 2y; 2x|− 3y^{2}]_{x_{0}}^{− 1}[x^{4} − y^{2} + 5; x^{2} − y^{3} + 1]_{x_{0}}; = [1; 1] − [4(1)^{3}|− 2(1); 2(1)|− 3(1)^{2}]^{− 1}[(1)^{4} − (1)^{2} + 5; (1)^{2} − (1)^{3} + 1]; = [1; 1] − [4|− 2; 2|− 3]^{− 1}[5; 1]; = [1; 1] − (1)/(4 ⋅ (− 3) − (− 2) ⋅ 2)[− 3|2; − 2|4][5; 1]; = [1; 1] + (1)/(8)[− 13; − 6]; = [− 0.625; 0.25].]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Alternative to Newton's Method for Multivariable Functions Using Linear Systems

Content:
Now that we’ve seen how to apply Newton’s method in the multivariable case, it’s worth noting that the standard update formula
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]

Item 14 — Tutorial: Derivation of the Formula

Content:
Just like in the single-variable case, the idea is to simplify the problem by replacing a nonlinear function with its linear approximation near our current guess.

Content:
Suppose we want to solve a system of nonlinear equations
[MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0},]
where [MATH: \boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n] is a vector-valued function.

Content:
Near a point [MATH: \mathbf{x}_0], we approximate [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})] using its first-order Taylor expansion:
[MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}) \approx \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) + J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0),]
where [MATH: J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)] is the Jacobian matrix of [MATH: \boldsymbol{f}] evaluated at [MATH: \mathbf{x}_0].

Content:
Since this linear approximation is valid near [MATH: \mathbf{x}_0], we solve the simpler system
[MATH: \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) + J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{0}]
instead of the full nonlinear system.

Content:
To find the next guess [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1], we solve this linear system for [MATH: \mathbf{x}]. We isolate the term [MATH: \mathbf{x}], as follows:

Content:
[MATH: J_{f}(x_{0})(x − x_{0})|= − f(x_{0}); x − x_{0}|= − [J_{f}(x_{0})]^{− 1}f(x_{0}); x|= x_{0} − [J_{f}(x_{0})]^{− 1}f(x_{0})]

Content:
This new value becomes our next guess, which we call [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1]. So, we write
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n).]

Content:
This is the multivariable version of the Newton–Raphson update rule.
